text:
Then he went out into the city. Perhaps she was to be met, to be discovered; perhaps she was sitting in a carriage. He wandered about until evening.

Outside the theatre he saw her; he bowed, smiled and bowed, and she returned his greeting. He was about to step forward to her—it was only a few paces—when he sees that she is not alone; she has Otto with her, the chamberlain’s son. He was in a lieutenant’s uniform.

Johannes thought: perhaps now she will give me a hint, a little sign with her eyes? She hurried into the theatre, red, with bowed head, as though she wished to hide.

Perhaps he could see her in there? He obtained a ticket and went in.

He knew about the chamberlain’s box; yes indeed, these rich people had a box. There she sat in all her splendour and looked about her. Did she look at him? Never!

When the act was over, he waited for her out in the corridor. He bowed again; she looked at him with a little surprise and nodded.

It is in here that you can get water, said Otto, pointing ahead.

They went past.

Johannes looked after them. A strange dimness settled before his eyes. All these people were angry with him and jostled him; he mechanically begged their pardon and remained standing. There she disappeared.

When she came back, he bowed deeply to her and said:

Excuse me, miss.

Otto answered and looked at him through narrowed eyes.

This is Johannes, she said by way of introduction. Do you remember him?

You presumably wish to know how things are at home, she continued, and her face was beautiful and calm. I really do not know, but I am sure all is well. Excellent. I shall give the miller’s family your regards.

Thank you. Will you be leaving soon, miss?

One of these days. Yes, I shall give them your regards.

She nodded and left.

Johannes again looked after her until she had disappeared, then went outside. An endless wandering, a heavy and sorrowful tramping up one street and down another, killed the time. At ten o’clock he stood outside the chamberlain’s house and waited. The theatres would soon be letting out; now she would come. Perhaps he could open the carriage door, take off his hat, open the carriage door and bow himself to the ground.

At last, half an hour later, she came. Could he remain standing there by the gate and once more bring himself to her notice? He hurried up the street and did not look back. He heard the gate at the chamberlain’s house open, the carriage drive in and the gate slam shut again. Then he turned around.

Now he continued pacing back and forth in front of the house for an hour. He was waiting for no one and had no errand. Suddenly the gate opens from within and Victoria steps out into the street again. She has no hat on and has merely thrown a shawl over her shoulders. She smiles, half frightened, half embarrassed, and begins by asking:

Are you walking here thinking?

No, he answers. Am I thinking? No, I am only walking here.

I saw you walking up and down out here, and so I wanted to.... I saw you from my window. I must go back in at once.

Thank you for coming, Victoria. I was so desperate a little while ago, and now it is over. Forgive me for greeting you at the theatre; unfortunately I have also asked for you here at the chamberlain’s house. I wanted to meet you and learn what you meant, what your opinion is.

Yes, she said, you already know that. I said so much the day before yesterday that you could not have misunderstood it.

I am still just as uncertain about everything.

Let us not speak of it any more. I have said enough; I have said far too much, and I am hurting you now. I love you. I did not lie the day before yesterday and I am not lying now; but there is so much that separates us. I am very fond of you, I like speaking with you, with you rather than with anyone else, but.... Yes, I dare not stand here any longer; they can see us from the windows. Johannes, there are so many reasons that you do not know, so you must not ask me any more to say what I mean. I have thought about it night and day; I mean what I have said. But it will be impossible.

What will be impossible?

The whole thing. All of it. Listen, Johannes, spare me from having to be proud for both of us.

Very well. Good, you shall be spared that! But then you deceived me the day before yesterday. What happened was that you met me in the street and then you were in good spirits and then....

She turned and was about to go inside.

Have I done something wrong? he asked. His face was pale and unrecognisable. I mean, by what have I forfeited your....? During these two days and two nights, have I committed some offence?

No. That is not it. I have merely thought it over; have you not? It has been impossible all along, you know. I am fond of you, esteem you....

And respect me.

She looks at him; his smile wounds her, and she continues more vehemently:

My God, do you not understand for yourself that Papa would refuse you that? Why do you force me to say it? You understand it yourself. What could it have come to? Am I not right?

A pause.

Yes, he answers.

Besides, she continues, there are so many reasons.... No, you really must not follow me to the theatre any more; I became frightened of you. You must never do that again.

No, he says.

She takes his hand.

Could you not come home for a visit? I should be very glad of it. How warm your hand is; I am freezing. No, now I must go. Good night.

Good night, he answers.

The street lay cold and grey uphill through the city; it looked like a belt of sand, an endless road to walk. He came upon a boy selling old, ruined roses; he called to him, took a rose, gave the boy a tiny five-kroner gold coin as a gift, and walked on. Shortly afterward he saw a cluster of children playing by a gate. A ten-year-old boy sits quietly watching; he has old blue eyes that follow the game, hollow cheeks and a square chin, and on his head he wore a cap of canvas. It was the lining of a cap. This child wore a wig; a disease of the hair had disfigured this head for good. Perhaps his soul too was utterly withered.

He noticed all this although he had no clear notion of which part of the city he was in or where he was going. It began to rain as well; he did not notice it and did not put up his umbrella, although he had carried it with him all day.

When at last he came to a square where there were benches, he went over and sat down. It rained more and more; unconsciously he put up the umbrella and remained sitting. After a short while an irresistible drowsiness came over him; his brain lay in a fog, he closed his eyes and began to nod and sleep.

After a while he awoke when some passers-by spoke loudly. He rose and drifted onward. His brain had grown clearer; he remembered what had happened, every event, even the boy to whom he had given five kroner for a rose. He imagined the little gentleman’s delight when he discovered this remarkable coin among his small change, that it was not a twenty-five-øre piece, but a five-kroner gold coin. Go with God!
